name: Malcolm X
role: American Muslim minister and Black nationalist leader; founder of Muslim Mosque, Inc. and the Organization of Afro-American Unity (assassinated 1965)
summary: Malcolm X spoke for Black self-determination, community control of politics, schools and economy, and the right of armed self-defence where government failed to protect Black Americans. After leaving the Nation of Islam in March 1964 and making the Hajj he dropped its racial separatism and white-devil doctrine, built a pan-African, human-rights framed movement and spoke of racism as a global problem, while still excluding whites from membership of his organisation. His economic remarks in 1964-65 criticised capitalism and said he favoured whatever served Black people, but he proposed no economic system.

notes: Positions follow the most recent clear statements (April 1964 to February 1965). Before the break with the Nation of Islam (to March 1964) he advocated racial separation and a separate Black state; Message to the Grass Roots (Nov 1963) is used only where consistent with later statements. The Hajj letter (April 1964) shows him revising earlier views on white people; the OAAU, however, admitted only people of African descent, and Wikipedia reports he began reconsidering black nationalism in his last months. On capitalism and socialism he made late remarks that capitalism was to blame for racism and that he would favour socialism if it helped Black people (Wikipedia), but no statement in the texts opened matches a specific statement, so those are null. The Oxford Union speech (Dec 1964), 'Malcolm X Speaks', the 1965 interviews and the Autobiography could not be opened as full text, so Vietnam, women, family and several other topics are null. The OAAU program page carries no date; the OAAU charter text was read by Malcolm X at the June 1964 rally.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Inferred: he called drug addiction and trafficking an evil to be eliminated from the community (OAAU, June 1964), while treating addicts as victims who need clinics; he did not discuss legalisation.

limit-guns.rationale: Defended the constitutional right to own rifles and shotguns (Ballot or the Bullet, April 1964) and in the OAAU charter said it would 'not give up a single right' to bear arms; said that if the government objected, it should disarm the racists rather than restrict Black owners. Applies to the general question of strict limits only by implication.

empower-police-military.rationale: On the OAAU platform (June 1964) he argued that adding police in Harlem had not reduced crime ('the more cops we have, the more crime we have') and called for a struggle against police brutality; he said some police were good but did not ask for more police power.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Inferred: the OAAU speech (June 1964) listed organised prostitution among vices destroying the community's moral fiber that it had to eliminate; legal status of consensual sex work was not discussed.

decide-locally.rationale: Black nationalism as he defined it in 1964 meant community control of local politics, economy and schools; the OAAU asked that Harlem schools be run by the Afro-American community and local school boards be influenced by it. This is community control, not a general argument about levels of government.

more-religion-public.rationale: Mixed: he said religion was his personal business and made the OAAU nonsectarian, but in his Mecca letter he held up Islam as the proven remedy for America's race problem.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Described civil rights as 'collecting for our investment' of 310 years of unpaid labour (Ballot or the Bullet) and said the only legislation worth endorsing is a 'Proclamation of Restitution' (OAAU program).

empower-international-orgs.rationale: The OAAU's first stated aim was to take the Black American problem to the UN under its human-rights declaration and charter, since the US government could not solve it; he did not argue for increasing UN powers generally.

revolution-justified.rationale: In 'The Black Revolution' (April 1964) and Ballot or the Bullet he spoke of revolutions that overturn systems and said that if Black Americans were denied the ballot they would turn to the bullet; in Message to the Grass Roots (Nov 1963) he said 'there is no such thing as a nonviolent revolution'. He also said a bloodless change was possible if Black citizens got full use of the ballot.

political-violence-never.rationale: In 1964-65 he said nonviolence should be kept for those who are nonviolent in return, asked for 'freedom by any means necessary', and described armed self-defence and a possible 'bullet' as justified if the ballot is denied.

separate-church-state.rationale: Said his religion was his 'personal business' and organised the OAAU as non-sectarian, separate from his religious group, the Muslim Mosque; he did not discuss church-state law.

direct-action.rationale: Points both ways: he urged mass voter registration, independent candidates and political clubs (OAAU, 1964) while also backing rent strikes and direct protest and warning that the ballot may fail.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Argued that textbooks, anthropology and the education system were shaped by the powerful to justify slavery and colonial rule and keep Black Americans mentally subordinate (OAAU program, Jan 1965 talk).

jewish-state-israel.rationale: In 'Zionist Logic' (Sept 1964) he argued the Zionist claim to Palestine had 'no intelligent or legal basis in history' and denied a legal or moral right to invade Arab Palestine on religious grounds. Wikipedia reports later 1965 remarks calling for a 'whole Palestine'.

national-self-determination.rationale: Praised African independence from colonial rule, and the OAAU program expresses 'sympathy and admiration for all peoples and nations' striving for self-realisation and complete freedom from oppression.

dominated-front.rationale: In Message to the Grass Roots (Nov 1963) he held up the 1955 Bandung conference of Asian and African nations, without whites, as a model; in January 1965 he described the Afro-Asian-Arab-Latin blocs approvingly as dark-skinned nations uniting against Western powers in the UN.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Opposed legally enforced segregation: in Ballot or the Bullet he said he was against a segregated school system and demanded civil rights 'now', and the OAAU memorandum and program attack America for preaching integration while practising segregation. His own separation proposals of the Nation of Islam period were for voluntary separation and self-governance, not segregation by law.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Described white politicians as 'political crooks' whose false promises and filibuster 'con game' failed Black voters (Ballot or the Bullet) and said both parties had sold Black Americans out (OAAU speech).

security-forces-accountable.rationale: The OAAU called for an 'unrelenting struggle against police brutality' and for taking the treatment of Black Americans, including unpunished lynchings and police violence, to the UN to 'indict Uncle Sam'. Applies to accountability for state security forces in general only in part.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Inferred: the OAAU program says that 'ethnic intermingling can be beneficial to all' when people have real equality and justice, and his Mecca letter shows regret for earlier views; he did not address marriage across racial lines directly after leaving the Nation of Islam in the sources used.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: OAAU program (1964-65) states that human rights are inalienable and belong to all people 'through God'; his Mecca letter describes the 'Oneness of Man' and rejects judging people by color.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: In 'Zionist Logic' (Egyptian Gazette, Sept 1964) he described Israel's occupation of Arab Palestine as a new form of colonialism that had uprooted its Arab citizens and seized their property.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: The OAAU speech backed city-wide rent strikes and demonstrations without seeking permission; the law on strikes was not discussed.

recall-officials.rationale: In the OAAU speech (June 1964) he said that 'any time the politician is not doing his job, we remove him', and supported only office-holders who answer to the Afro-American community. It is unclear whether he meant recall during a term or removal by election.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Argued that the colonial powers' scientific and anthropological claims were made to justify domination and that African history and culture had been hidden; the OAAU program voices admiration for all peoples. He stressed the greatness of African civilisation more than formal equality of all cultures.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: The OAAU aimed to unite all people of African descent in the Western Hemisphere and then with Africa, modelled on the Organization of African Unity; 'we have one destiny and we've had one past'.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: In 1964-65 he called for Afro-American community-run schools, a cultural center and a 'cultural revolution' inside the United States rather than a separate Black state; a separate state had been the Nation of Islam goal he left behind.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: From 1964 the OAAU programme centred on registering voters, independent political clubs, control of local schools and a UN human-rights petition in the United States, rather than emigration; it also asked for cultural and economic ties with Africa and travel there.

history-own-civilization.rationale: The OAAU called for Black-written textbooks, liberation schools and control of Harlem schools to teach African and Afro-American history; applied to Black American and African history rather than to a state's national history.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Rejected colonial rule and the 'scientific' justifications for European domination of Africans and Asians (Jan 1965 talk; OAAU speech).

recallable-delegates.rationale: Same OAAU remarks (June 1964): support only for office-holders 'responsible to the Afro-American community' and removal of any who fail; the mechanism is not specified.

religion-illusion.rationale: A practising Muslim after the Hajj who wrote that Islam 'erases from its society the race problem' and that America needs to understand it; he did not treat religion as an illusion.

historical-land-claim.rationale: In 'Zionist Logic' he rejected a claim to land based on forefathers living there thousands of years ago, comparing it to a hypothetical Moorish claim to Spain.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Condemned colonialism and neo-imperial economic exploitation in Africa (OAAU speech, Zionist Logic, 1964).

participatory-democracy.rationale: The OAAU speech urged organising block by block, parent involvement in every phase of school life and community-run schools and anti-vice work; the program encouraged each member to take part in committees. Applies to community and school decisions rather than workplaces or universities generally.

islam-incompatible.rationale: His 1964 Mecca letter says America needs to understand Islam and proposes it as a solution to American racism; he did not regard it as incompatible with the West.

property-franchise.rationale: Demanded the ballot for every Black American and said 'a man has a right to vote, a man has a right to be registered'; he did not discuss property qualifications specifically.

racial-franchise.rationale: Demanded that Black Americans get 'full use of the ballot in every one of the 50 states' and said anyone who stops people registering is breaking the law; the OAAU launched a voter registration drive.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: No stated position on the state promoting atheism; his being a practising Muslim is a label, not a view on state policy.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Mixed: the OAAU said the community should do the major part of charity work itself, while also urging Black veterans and others to claim every government benefit they are entitled to.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: The OAAU charter he read out (June 1964) asserts 'since self-preservation is the first law of nature' a right and obligation of self-defence, 'a man with a rifle or a club can only be stopped by a person who defends himself with a rifle or a club'.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: The OAAU program urged cultural, communications, technical and travel links with Africa while campaigning in the US, rather than a general return of Black Americans.

racial-group-interests.rationale: The OAAU (June 1964) was open only to people of African descent, with whites invited to organise separately in the white community; its program states 'the exclusive ethnic quality of our unity is necessary for self-preservation' while saying it is 'not opposed to multiethnic associations'. Wikipedia reports he began to reconsider black nationalism in his last months, but no clear statement of that is in the sources used.

racial-pride.rationale: 'A race of people is like an individual man; until it uses its own talent, takes pride in its own history, expresses its own culture, affirms its own selfhood, it can never fulfill itself' (OAAU speech, June 1964); the program calls for a cultural revolution to restore identity.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: The OAAU charter (June 1964) asserted that Black communities may defend themselves 'by whatever means necessary' where the government will not protect them, and set up a self-defence committee; he did not accept that only state forces may bear arms.

premarital-sex.rationale: Inferred: in 'The Black Revolution' (April 1964) he listed adultery leading to children born outside marriage among the social evils to be eliminated, while the OAAU speech called for help for unwed mothers; no direct statement on sex outside marriage for women.

race-social-construct.rationale: In his January 1965 Harlem talk he argued that the racial categories of 'Mongoloid, Caucasoid and Negroid' were drawn by anthropologists acting as agents of colonial powers to justify domination, and that who counts as 'Negroid' was assigned inconsistently. The OAAU program calls 'racial' differences artificially created. He did not rule out biological claims in so many words.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: Wanted the Black majority in Harlem and similar districts to control their own politics, economy and schools; this was described as community control, not formal territorial autonomy.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Founded the OAAU for the non-Muslim majority of Afro-Americans 'whatever their ideology', explicitly nonsectarian, and kept religion in the separate Muslim Mosque Inc.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: Stated throughout 1964-65 that racism in America was an 'incurable cancer' (Mecca letter) and the system a racist power structure that kept Black Americans in 'slavery' (OAAU program).
